source.title: Efficient Training of Language Models to Fill in the Middle
source.authors: Mo Bavarian; Heewoo Jun; N. Tezak; John D. Schulman; Christine McLeavey; Jerry Tworek; Mark Chen

record.tranche_reason: The study measures held-out autoregressive test loss across model sizes, but does not fit or evaluate the original scaling-law equations.
record.gate_note: The paper reports parameter-scale loss curves for FIM-trained and ordinary autoregressive models. It does not fit power laws, report exponents, test extrapolation from smaller runs, or study compute-optimal allocation. Downstream benchmark evaluations are not recorded as findings about predictable scale trends.
record.test_reason: This is a fill-in-the-middle (FIM) training paper. It plots left-to-right test loss against non-embedding parameters (50M–6.9B, fixed 100B tokens) only to show FIM and AR models follow the same curve ("FIM-for-free"). It fits no power law, reports no exponents, does no extrapolation and studies no allocation. The scaling plots serve as a tool for comparing its own training method, not as a test of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct but incomplete. The authors conclude that FIM can be learned 'for free' in pretraining: left-to-right loss and benchmarks are unaffected for FIM rates below 100%, while FIM loss and infilling improve. They also conclude that learning FIM by finetuning is compute-inefficient, that perplexity does not reflect infilling performance, and that character-level, context-level, joint PSM/SPM training at 50–90% FIM rate works best. They draw no conclusion about scaling-law form or allocation.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares test-loss curves over model sizes but does not reproduce the original scaling-law fitting procedure or report fitted laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Ordinary autoregressive test loss shows no noticeable degradation through a 90% FIM rate, but degrades at a 100% rate. The paper also notes that the largest models in the fixed-token runs may be undertrained.

fits_no_version.finding: A 50% FIM rate leaves the left-to-right test-loss trend over model size unchanged in both language and code (Fig. 1). Up to 90% FIM shows no degradation; 100% FIM degrades AR loss (Figs. 4, 12).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Mixing FIM-transformed data into pretraining (below 100%) does not shift the AR loss-vs-size scaling curve.

fits_no_version.finding: FIM rate and context- vs document-level FIM change FIM test loss negligibly (about 0.001 nats/token), yet change infilling pass rates substantially and can change the slope of pass-rate scaling trends (Sec. 4.2, 4.4, App. B). The authors say loss-only scaling analysis is misleading here.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Across training-configuration choices at equal loss, sampling-based task performance can differ greatly, so loss does not predict task performance across such choices.

record.problems: The loss values are presented in figures without tabulated numerical values or fitted exponents. All main model runs use a fixed 100B-token horizon, and the authors expect the largest models to be undertrained.

untested.parts: No power-law form, fit or exponent. The study varies only parameters at fixed 100B tokens, with the largest models undertrained.
Downstream benchmarks vs scale are plotted (Fig. 3, Fig. 13) only to compare FIM and AR. Predictability with scale or loss is not assessed.

record.verdict_notes: The paper follows Kaplan in using non-embedding parameters on its scaling plots and cites Hoffmann to note its largest models are undertrained. These citations are not tests. The record's 'tests/T2' classification is wrong; it should be uses_without_test/T4.

versions.untested_parts: The study varies parameter count at a fixed 100B-token training horizon, but does not establish a power-law form, fit exponents, or test scaling with tokens or compute. It notes that the largest models may be undertrained.

rows.check: The row compares the study's own method (50% FIM) with an AR baseline. It does not measure whether loss follows a power law in parameters. No fit or exponent is given, and all runs use a fixed 100B-token horizon with the largest models undertrained, so the 'other factors not the bottleneck' condition of V1 is not met.
